comment: As someone who attended all of the interviews for the Planning Commission seats, I believe there were multiple candidates which had valuable experience and a strong desire to serve our community. I fully supported the appointments which were made. At our Mayor's suggestion, the Planning Department has been asked to prepare an amendment to the LMC to include more specific criteria as a requirement for the Planning Commission. I have a couple of thoughts I hope you will give consideration. 1) Does the City have a professional(s) in the engineering or building department with experience not limited to construction, planning or architecture which reviews applications and provides the appropriate scrutiny, calculations, analysis, etc. to the Planning Staff to include in their staff reports? Including this as part of the review process and putting their findings and/or conclusions in the staff report would lend additional confidence to the staff recommendations to the Commission. This individual should also be available to the Planning Commissioners should they have additional questions or concerns as they review the packet or discuss the application during the meeting. While references have been made in previous staff reports to various departments reviewing and giving their input on feasibility, if the City does not have an employee(s) with the necessary qualifications to perform this important aspect of review, perhaps it is a new position which should be considered rather than trying to find a member of the community to fill this role as part of their duty as a Commissioner. 2) Based on the wording of the amendment, it would seem anyone with professional experience not limited to construction, planning or architecture would automatically tick a box and have a leg up even if they are overall less qualified than someone without this professional experience. And, just because someone has professional experience does not guarantee that it is "good" experience. For example, someone may have experience as an accountant yet still produce inaccurate financial statements which potentially results in big issues, financially, legally or otherwise. As always, I appreciate your service to our community.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: Winter routing, currently 2 Green. For years the bus coming west bound on Holiday Ranch would cross 224 at the light and then in about 50 feet make a left turn on to Prospector Dr. This has increased safety aspects. Rather than sit blocking traffic, as a bus needs greater leeway when making left turns, they crossed over via the through traffic lane. Making a left turn on 224 to include immediate transition to the right shoulder and stop location, utilize the next available left turn off PayDay in a very low traffic environment, onto Prospector enabled the bus to provide service to additional neighborhood stops. At the south end of Prospector the bus services a protected stop before making a right turn onto 224 to rejoin the route. The safety enhancement was also that we did not have to stand essentially on the shoulder of an extremely busy 224 waiting for a bus. In winter snow conditions this is a very dangerous option. If the city wants residents to use the bus transit system you will need to consider what works for us as well. The alternative is to just use a car to go everywhere.

comment: Unfortunately we are unable to attend the meeting in person on Thursday evening but we would like to make our thoughts known as people who live near and utilize the rail trail almost daily in all capacities. 1. We are supportive of all the improvements around the creek and making that area look nice with more benches, etc. 2. We also appreciate more signage to remind people that this is a shared trail among children, dogs, pedestrians, bikes and e-bikes, and the speeds have to be maintained and the bikes (of all kinds) need to yield to all others. 3. We do NOT agree that the trail should be widened at this point. The wider the trail, the more people will use it, and they will go even faster than they do now. In the last 2 years we have seen the rail trail change into a small highway filled with speeding e-bikes, young children operating these e-bikes, accidents and injuries among locals and visitors. It is not safe for the riders or the pedestrians. We are all for more biking and walking and less traffic from vehicles, but from what we have seen firsthand, if the rail trail is widened, it could quickly become a feeding ground for ER visits. Thank you for the hard work that you do, and for your consideration.

comment: I would like to restate my concerns RE the Rail Trail Master Plan and to reiterate my urgent wildlife request. Widening trails will just attract more speeding and have possible negative impacts on habitats and wildlife. PC has excellent bike lanes on its roads. On the rail trail we should encourage people to slow & look around. I love the idea of birdhouses stationed along the trail!! As part of the tree planting program, why not plant bushes such as crabapple on public land near the rail trail so people can watch deer, moose, elk and birds harvest them? The rail trails should be for people to spend time in nature and hopefully be able to see wildlife, esp moose! The shocking relocation of the mother moose and her baby from Prospector Park this week should never, ever be allowed to happen again! The council needs to step up to the plate and send a strong message. I request that you draw up a document to state to the public and esp. DNR that Park City‘s counsel stands firmly against the relocation of our large wildlife. Unless it can be unequivocally proven to police and DNR that said wildlife presents unprovoked danger to people, they must be left in their habitat. The greatest gift that we can give future generations is protecting our wildlife and preserving our environment for people to experience in as natural a state as possible.

comment: The plan focuses too much on creating a new transportation corridor focused primarily on ebikes and not enough on preserving the peaceful park-like amenity we have now. The rail trail is a park with a mixed-use path, not an alternative transportation artery. Hyping that aspect is how we begin, I think. The rail trail is a friendly place. Cyclists must always yield to pedestrians. Dogs should be leashed or under voice control. Other towns have done a lot of work on this, let’s look at what they’ve done before we cut down our trees, grade the trailside, and free the cyclists to go as fast as they like. The proposal timeline sensibly begins with the lowhanging fruit, some of which has already begun to show up: Maintenance Striping Wayfinding signage There is no funding for the major and most expensive, disruptive proposals that are a few years down the road, the widening, bridge building, expansion, wetlands issues, restrooms, etc. I suggest we begin with more of the low hanging fruit while the required studies go forward: Along the way show people the extent of the proposed expansion and THEN ask them if they like that idea. The striping is a gentle reminder to share the trail. More trash cans and pet waste bags (and a realistic maintenance schedule) will help keep the trail clean. The Wag’On Trail is a great idea. Signage reminding dog owners to leash their animals and pick up after them will also help. Concerns: The proposed cross section is too large and unnecessarily trades trees, grasses, and other plants for road base. Designating all paved surface for cycling will result in greater speed and more danger to pedestrians for the inevitable conflicts. Traffic calming involves reducing perceived space. PC spends a lot of effort on it elsewhere. The proposal is the exact opposite. Preserving natural habitats should always be a priority in PC.

comment: On the Park City Council (PCC) will vote on a proposal to widen the Union Pacific rail trail by 8 feet of asphalt and 4 feet of gravel between Bonanza Drive, Wyatt Earp Way, and State route 248 east of US-40. The proposed widening includes making the asphalt pathway 18 feet wide with 2 feet of gravel on either side, for a total width of 22 feet. According to Summit County regulations “Access roads shall be limited to ten feet (10’) in width” (11-6-8: INFRASTRUCTURE STANDARDS; https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/ summitcountyut/latest/summitcounty_ut/0-0-0-18970). Widening the rail trail therefore will turn it from a trail into a road. Below are a few of the reasons and issues that must be addressed before either widening the rail trail or making other changes. 1. There is a vibrant eco system of ducks, geese, herons, resident and migrating birds (e.g. pelicans), beavers, muskrats, ground squirrels, and flora in the wetlands on the north side of the rail trail between Wyatt Earp Way and State route 248. Moose and deer come down from the south side hills to drink at the wetlands and sandhill cranes travel along the rail trail and the berm in spring with their young. There has been no consideration of how widening the trail (including replacing existing bridges over water) will impact the flora and fauna. An environmental impact study of the wetlands is essential before any changes are made to the trail. 2. There are many mature trees within 10-12 feet of the trail on the south side of the rail trail east of Wyatt Earp Way. These trees sit on a berm. Widening the trail by any amount (proposal is for 8 feet) on the south side of the existing trail will require cutting down part of the berm and is likely to impact (kill?) these mature trees by eliminating and/or cutting their roots. These trees provide an important barrier between the rail trail and houses along the south side of the trail. 3. Off-leash dogs climb the berm and defecate in the backyards of the houses on the south side of the rail trail. Dog owners are usually unaware of this activity so the clean-up is left to the homeowners. Widening the trail on the south side will make it easier for off-leash dogs to find a location to defecate. 4. Widening the trail will not stop bikers from speeding. Traffic calming guidelines involve narrowing, not widening roads. A divider for walkers vs bikers will not stop folks from biking/walking on the wrong side since it’s unlikely people will adhere to directions (or if they’ll even read the directions). Most bikers currently do not stop at stop signs.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)
